citations.quote: a real matrix $G\in\mathbb R^{p\times m}$ maps coefficients $a\in\mathbb R^m$ to predicted observations $Ga$.
there exists a unique non-negative operator $R:V\to V$ such that $$R^2=T.$$
there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and $(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$

derivations.claim: Since $R\succ0$, it is positive semidefinite, so [F1] gives a symmetric positive-semidefinite $S$ with $S^2=R$. If $Sv=0$, then $Rv=S^2v=0$, and positive definiteness of $R$ forces $v=0$; hence $S$ is invertible. Therefore $W=S^{-1}$ is symmetric positive definite and $W^TW=S^{-2}=R^{-1}$.

Apply [F2] to $A$ on the nonzero finite-dimensional inner-product space $E$: for an orthonormal basis $e_1,\ldots,e_d$ of $E$, the SVD gives $r\le\min(d,p)$ positive singular values $s_1,\ldots,s_r$, an orthonormal list $f_1,\ldots,f_r$ in $\mathbb R^p$, $Ae_i=s_if_i$ for $i\le r$, and $Ae_i=0$ for $i>r$. For $v=\sum_i c_ie_i$ with $\|v\|_2=1$, $\|Av\|_2^2=\sum_{i=1}^r s_i^2c_i^2$. Thus the infimum in the Statement is zero when $r<d$ and is $\min_i s_i$ when $r=d$; it is positive exactly when $A$ is injective. If $r<d$, any $e_j$ with $j>r$ is a nonzero kernel vector.

The operator $W$ is invertible by step 1.1, so for every $v\in E$, $Av=0$ if and only if $WGv=0$, which holds if and only if $Gv=0$. Thus $A$ is injective exactly when $G|_E$ is injective, and in the noninjective case a nonzero $v\in E\cap\ker G$ gives $G(a+v)=Ga$ for every $a\in E$. In the pressure-field case stated in the item, an additive-constant direction with $Gv_c=0$ is such a null vector. Restricting coefficients to a complement of its span fixes this direction, while identifying $a$ and $b$ when $a-b$ lies in that span gives the stated equivalence-class formulation.

Suppose $\sigma_{\min}(A)>0$. Step 1.2 then has $r=d\le p$, so the $d$ vectors $f_1,\ldots,f_d$ form an orthonormal list that extends to an orthonormal basis $f_1,\ldots,f_p$ of $\mathbb R^p$ by [F2]. For $y=Ga+e$, write $a=\sum_{i=1}^d a_ie_i$ and $Wy=\sum_{i=1}^d b_if_i+b_\perp$, where $b_\perp$ is orthogonal to each $f_i$ for $i\le d$. For any $b=\sum_{i=1}^d c_ie_i\in E$, $\|W(y-Gb)\|_2^2=\sum_{i=1}^d(b_i-s_ic_i)^2+\|b_\perp\|_2^2$; since each $s_i>0$, this is uniquely minimized by $c_i=b_i/s_i$. Therefore $\hat a-a=\sum_{i=1}^d s_i^{-1}\langle We,f_i\rangle e_i$. Orthonormality gives $\|\hat a-a\|_2^2=\sum_{i=1}^d s_i^{-2}|\langle We,f_i\rangle|^2\le\sigma_{\min}(A)^{-2}\sum_{i=1}^d|\langle We,f_i\rangle|^2\le\sigma_{\min}(A)^{-2}\|We\|_2^2$, where the last inequality follows by expanding $We$ in the full orthonormal basis. Taking square roots proves the bound.

risk_review.notes: Read all four current proof steps, exact square-root/SVD statements and their complete local proofs, and reader/refuter evidence. R positive definite makes its symmetric square root injective and invertible; W preserves kernels. On nonzero E the full domain singular-value list includes zeros when dim(E)>p or rank is deficient, so the unit-sphere infimum is attained and is positive iff G restricted to E is injective. Both directions checked. In the full-column-rank case, orthogonal expansion uniquely minimizes the squared weighted residual and yields the stated inverse-minimum-gain error bound by a finite sum of squared coordinates. Zero G, one-dimensional E, singular G and exact error zero are covered; E=0 is excluded. The pressure constant direction is defined by Pi and lies in ker(G); the complement fixes only this direction, and G descends to the quotient since its span is in the kernel. Neither construction asserts removal of other null directions. No stochastic error law, confidence statement or general PDE result follows. No new choice use. The only item consumer is the unchanged two-mode example, which uses the unchanged kernel conclusion. Axler fourth edition 7.65, 7.68 and 7.70 with proof (printed pp.271-274) support the singular-value convention; local square-root and SVD suppliers furnish the exact results. No unresolved defect.

derivations.claim: Direct multiplication gives $G(a_1,a_2)^T=a_1$ and $G(0,1)^T=0$, while $(0,1)^T\ne0$. Thus $v=(0,1)^T$ is a nonzero vector in the kernel of $G$.

For every $a\in\mathbb R^2$ and every $t\in\mathbb R$, linearity gives $G(a+tv)=Ga+tGv=Ga$. Taking any $t\ne0$ produces a distinct coefficient vector with the same predicted observation and the same realized error $e$; by [F1], the coefficient vector is not identifiable.
